11   Q6.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY?

13         base-rate revenue allocation, as supported by the Class Cost-of-Service ("CCOS")

14         study, including the proposal to phase in the requested base-rate revenue increase

15         to mitigate the bill impact on certain classes. It describes EPE's rate design based

19         use rate structure across rate classes that have the capability to shift usage from the

20         system peak period; and I present EPE’s request to implement a Peak Time Rebate

21         Pilot Program. Finally, I support two proposed new large load tariff schedules.

17             THE PROPOSED RATE DESIGN PRESENTED IN THIS CASE?

18   A.        EPE seeks to achieve a variety of goals through its proposed rate design. These

12   Q16. HOW DOES THE COMPANY PROPOSE TO MINIMIZE SUBSIDIES

13        WITHIN EACH RATE CLASS?

14   A.   Subsidies within a rate class occur when the components of the rates charged do

15        not adequately reflect the underlying costs to serve that rate class. EPE proposes

16        to minimize intra-rate class subsidies, to the extent possible, by ensuring that the

17        proposed rates adequately recover each classification component cost in a manner

18        that appropriately reflects their cost causation. Recovering costs based on rate

19        components that reasonably reflect their cost causation results in price efficiency

20        and reduces the potential that some customers within a rate class will subsidize

 3   Q17. PLEASE DESCRIBE, IN GENERAL, THESE RATE COMPONENTS.

 4   A.   For non-lighting rate classes, the rate components commonly used for the recovery

 5        of costs consist of customer charges, energy charges, and demand charges. A

 6        customer charge is a fixed monthly charge that recovers costs incurred in making

 7        service available at the customer’s premise such as meter and meter reading costs,

 8        billing, record keeping, customer service, and an apportioned share of

 9        administration and general costs. Energy charges recover costs that vary with the

10        amount of electricity consumed such as fuel, purchased power, variable operation

11        and maintenance costs, and an apportioned share of administration and general

12        costs. For rate classes that are not billed demand charges, the energy charge is

13        designed to recover the costs typically recovered through demand charges. An

14        energy charge is applied on a kilowatt hour ("kWh") basis and increases

15        proportionally with the customer’s total energy usage during the billing period.

16        Finally, a demand charge is designed to recover capacity-related costs, such as

17        generation, transmission, and distribution infrastructure needed to meet the

18        customer’s maximum demand on the system, and an apportioned share of

19        administration and general costs. It is typically applied based on the customer’s

20        highest measured average kilowatt ("kW") demand during the billing period or

21        designated peak hours.

 2   Q18. IS EPE PROPOSING RATE STRUCTURES THAT ENCOURAGE

 3        ENERGY         CONSERVATION                AND      POTENTIALLY            REDUCE

 4        CUSTOMERS’ CONTRIBUTION TO EPE’S SYSTEM PEAK?

 5   A.   Yes. Accurate price signals convey to customers the cost differences between

 6        seasonal and non-seasonal time periods. This allows customers to make economic

 7        decisions, promotes energy conservation, and encourages customers to shift usage

 8        from peak periods to off-peak periods. EPE’s proposed demand and energy charges

 9        are intended to produce accurate price signals that communicate those price

10        differentials to customers, particularly during summer months. For those rate

11        classes with a time variant pricing structure (i.e., time of use rates), energy charges

12        are developed with on-peak period energy price differentials that have the

13        incentivizing effect of reducing contributions to EPE’s system peak.

14

15   Q19. DO EPE’S PROPOSED RATES ENHANCE RATE STABILITY FOR

16        CUSTOMERS?

17   A.   Yes. Because EPE’s costs of service and cost responsibility by rate class generally

18        do not vary widely from year-to-year, cost-based rates should be similarly stable,

19        avoiding significant rate volatility for customers. Rates that closely follow their

20        underlying cost provide customers with accurate price signals, which allow

21        customers to reasonably anticipate what their electric bills will be and make

 3   Q20. DO THE PROPOSED RATES PROMOTE STABILITY OF REVENUES

4         FOR EPE?

 5   A.   Yes. The proposed rates link revenues more closely to costs, thereby ensuring that

 6        the costs are reasonably matched with revenues. That is, by sending customers

 7        more accurate price signals, EPE anticipates that revenues will better track future

8         cost increases (or decreases). In addition, EPE’s proposed rates attempt to provide

 9        a more consistent recovery of fixed costs (i.e., costs that do not vary with the

10        amount of kWh consumed) through more accurate customer and demand charges.

11

12   Q21. HOW DO THE PROPOSED RATES PROVIDE EPE WITH AN

13        OPPORTUNITY TO RECOVER ITS COSTS?

14   A.   As demonstrated by Schedule O-2, Proof of Revenues, the proposed rates are designed

15        to fully recover EPE’s proposed revenue requirement of each phase. Furthermore, the

16        proposed rates link revenues more closely to costs, resulting in revenues that more

17        accurately track costs year over year.

18

 8   Q23. DESCRIBE EPE’S GENERAL PROCESS USED TO DESIGN ITS

 9        PROPOSED BASE RATES IN THIS CASE?

10   A.   Theoretically, rates can be developed following any sequence with respect to the

11        different cost elements. EPE chose to start the rate design process with the

12        determination of the customer charge for each rate class. As a general principle,

13        EPE targeted a customer charge that would allow for the recovery of 100% of the

14        customer-related costs for each rate class.

15               Next, if applicable, EPE proceeded with the design of the demand charges,

16        using EPE’s allocated production and transmission costs to recognize seasonal

18        participating customers will be notified by EPE in advance and given the

19        opportunity to voluntarily reduce their energy usage compared to their typical

20        consumption. If a customer reduces usage below their baseline during the event

21        window, they will earn a bill credit based on the avoided cost of energy described
